title: Masseter Muscle Volume and Cross‐Sectional Area as Risk Factors for Late Mechanical Dental Implant Failure: A Matched Case–Control Study
abstract: ABSTRACT Objectives This study aimed to investigate whether three‐dimensional (3D) masseter muscle morphology—volume and cross‐sectional area (CSA)—is associated with the risk of late mechanical dental implant failure and to derive preliminary cut‐off values for risk stratification. Material and Methods This 1:4 matched case–control study investigated 23 cases of late mechanical failure (fixture fracture, screw fracture, or abutment fracture) and 92 successful controls. Participants were matched by gender, age (±10 years), anatomical location, and maintenance period (±2 years). Masseter morphology was quantified using the 3D reconstruction of the cone‐beam computed tomography (CBCT) data. Independent risk factors were determined using a multivariable generalized estimating equation model adjusting for potential confounders. Results Increased masseter muscle bulk was significantly associated with mechanical failure ( p 3 increase in masseter volume and by 1.11‐fold per 10 mm 2 increase in CSA. ROC analysis demonstrated AUCs of 0.846 for masseter volume and 0.871 for CSA. The maximum‐Youden thresholds were 31,272.56 mm 3 for volume and 691.30 mm 2 for CSA, with sensitivities of 86.96% and 82.61% and specificities of 77.17% and 79.35%, respectively. Internal bootstrap validation yielded AUC 95% confidence intervals of 0.751–0.931 and 0.767–0.951, respectively. Conclusions Greater masseter muscle volume and CSA were significantly associated with late mechanical implant failure in this matched case–control study. The proposed cut‐off values may provide preliminary reference values for risk stratification. However, these findings should be regarded as exploratory and require prospective validation in independent cohorts before routine clinical implementation.

title: Intraoral Ultrasonography for Mid-Buccal Probing Depth Assessment: A Proof-of-Concept Clinical Agreement Study.
abstract: ABSTRACT Aim To evaluate the agreement between ultrasound‐derived gingival sulcus depth ( uGSD ) and clinical probing depth ( PD ) at standardised mid‐buccal sites as a proof‐of‐concept study. Materials and Methods Mid‐buccal measurements were obtained from 963 sites in 69 participants (767 anterior, 127 premolars, 69 first molars) using an 18‐MHz ultrasound transducer and a UNC‐15 probe. uGSD was measured on B‐mode images; reliability was assessed by two trained examiners. Agreement was evaluated using intra‐class correlation coefficient (ICC), Bland–Altman analysis and mean absolute error (MAE). Generalised estimating equations and clustered ICCs accounted for within‐patient clustering. Subgroups included PD strata, bleeding, tooth type, calculus, restorations (prosthetic crowns/orthodontic attachments) and smoking. Results Ultrasound measurements showed high reliability (ICCs > 0.90). Agreement between uGSD and clinical PD was strong (ICC = 0.942; 95% CI: 0.935–0.949), with negligible mean difference (+0.023 mm) and low MAE (0.29 ± 0.32 mm). Subgroup ICCs ranged from 0.786 to 0.952; 85.0% of sites differed by ≤ 0.50 mm and 96.7% by ≤ 1.00 mm. Molar sites showed the highest MAE (0.38 mm) and slight underestimation (−0.123 mm). Conclusion Intraoral ultrasonography showed high agreement with clinical PD at standardised mid‐buccal sites in anterior teeth, premolars and first molars. It may serve as a non‐invasive adjunct to conventional probing; however, broader studies are needed across complex sites and examiner experience levels.
